draft.title: The Day of Mourning
card: On 26 January 1938, Australians marked 150 years since the First Fleet arrived at Sydney in 1788. Many white Australians celebrated.
On the same day, Aboriginal activists held a meeting in Sydney, called the Day of Mourning. Leaders included William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson.
They protested against the way Aboriginal people were treated. They said 150 years of British settlement had brought loss of land, control over their lives and poor treatment.
They demanded equal rights, including full citizenship rights. The meeting showed that Aboriginal people were organising and speaking for themselves.
draft.remember: In 1938, Aboriginal leaders turned a day of celebration into a protest for equal rights.

a.q: Why did Aboriginal activists hold the Day of Mourning on 26 January 1938?
opts: To protest and demand equal rights while others celebrated
To join the celebrations and thank the government
To ask for the First Fleet's arrival to be repeated
To end the celebrations with a march through every state
a.why: The activists chose the day of the 150 year celebrations to draw attention to how Aboriginal people had been treated and to demand equal rights. They did not join the celebrations, because for them the day marked loss rather than a reason to celebrate.
a.clue: Think about what the day meant to them compared with other Australians.

b.q: Which person was a leader of the 1938 Day of Mourning meeting in Sydney?
opts: William Cooper
Charles Perkins
Gough Whitlam
Arthur Phillip
b.why: William Cooper was one of the Aboriginal activists who led the meeting, along with Jack Patten and William Ferguson. Charles Perkins is a tempting choice because he was also an Aboriginal activist, but he is linked to a different protest, and that was later.
b.clue: The card names three leaders. Pick the one from the card.

a.best: To protest and demand equal rights while others celebrated

The distractors are implausible for Year 10: 'To ask for the First Fleet's arrival to be repeated' and 'To join the celebrations and thank the government'. A student can pick the answer by elimination without understanding the idea.

'brought loss of land, control over their lives and poor treatment' is ambiguous. It can be read as settlement bringing 'control over their lives' rather than loss of control. Saying 'loss of land, loss of control over their lives and poor treatment' would make it clear.

proposal.title: The Day of Mourning
card: On 26 January 1938, Australians marked 150 years since the First Fleet arrived at Sydney in 1788. Many white Australians celebrated.
On the same day, Aboriginal activists held a meeting in Sydney, called the Day of Mourning. Leaders included William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson.
They protested against the way Aboriginal people were treated. They said 150 years of British settlement had brought loss of land, loss of control over their lives and poor treatment.
They demanded equal rights, including full citizenship rights. The meeting showed that Aboriginal people were organising and speaking for themselves.
proposal.remember: In 1938, Aboriginal leaders turned a day of celebration into a protest for equal rights.

a.q: Why did the activists choose 26 January 1938 for their meeting?
opts: It marked 150 years of loss since the First Fleet
It was the day the Commonwealth of Australia began
It was the day Aboriginal people first won the vote
It marked the end of 150 years of British rule
a.why: The date was the 150th anniversary of the First Fleet's arrival. Others celebrated it, but the activists saw those years as a time of lost land, lost control and poor treatment. The Commonwealth began in 1901, not 1938, and the day did not mark any rights being won.
a.clue: What had happened 150 years before that date?

b.q: A historian says the Day of Mourning mattered because Aboriginal people spoke for themselves. Which fact best supports this?
opts: Aboriginal activists organised and led the meeting
It was held on the 150th anniversary of settlement
Many white Australians celebrated on the same day
The meeting took place in the city of Sydney
b.why: The claim is about who was speaking, so the best support is that Aboriginal activists such as Cooper, Patten and Ferguson ran the meeting. The anniversary date is tempting because it explains why the day was chosen, but it says nothing about who led the protest.
b.clue: The claim is about who did the speaking, not when or where.
